idiom_name: wrapper that owns setup and teardown and takes the body as a function value
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: write one method whose parameters are the acquisition inputs plus the body (a function value, block or closure); inside it perform setup, invoke the body exactly once while the resource is live, then teardown on every exit path - normal return, early return, thrown error. Give it an intention-revealing name from the pair it encapsulates (openDuring:, withTransaction, readStreamWhile:), return the body's result, and decide and document the failure policy for a teardown that fails while the body is already failing. Keep the paired primitives private so callers cannot bypass the wrapper, and prefer the language's own bracket when one exists and no extra policy is needed.
code_sketch:
def with_resource(acquire_args, body):
    resource = acquire(acquire_args)      # setup
    try:
        return body(resource)             # body, exactly once
    finally:
        release(resource)                 # teardown on every exit path

# caller: with_resource(args, lambda r: work(r))
# teardown failure while the body fails needs an explicit policy: suppress, aggregate or log
pitfalls: Skipping the hand-off and letting the body see the raw protocol invites callers to re-open or re-close; keep the paired primitives out of the body's reach.
Invoking the body zero or several times (a wrapper that decides from a mode flag) turns the pattern into control coupling and breaks the guarantee callers read into the name.
Without a stated exception policy the wrapper silently reorders failures: the body's error disappears behind a teardown error, or the teardown error is dropped entirely.

Nested execute-around: two wrappers for the same resource in the same scope can deadlock or double-clean if they do not coordinate (e.g., two lock wrappers on the same mutex). Detect or document nesting restrictions.

Thread-safety gap: the wrapper may be thread-safe but the resource it hands to the body often is not; concurrent access to a pooled connection or file handle inside the body bypasses the wrapper's guarantees.
Debugging through layers: a stack trace through several nested execute-around wrappers obscures which body threw and what state the resource was in at the throw point.

Closure capture overhead: the body lambda/closure allocates on the heap in most languages, which matters in hot paths (tight loops, per-request handlers); profile before using the pattern in latency-critical code.

Parameter creep: wrappers attract modes, retry counts, timeouts and visitor callbacks until they are a different pattern wearing the wrapper's name — add a new wrapper name only when the guarantee changes, not when arguments do.

Wrong move: trusting a third-party wrapper to invoke your body exactly once -> inversion of control means the wrapper can run the body too early, twice, or never, and the guarantee callers read into the name silently breaks -> instead treat 'invoked exactly once on every path' as a tested API contract, and prefer brackets whose lifecycle the language enforces (using, with, defer, RAII).

Wrong move: reusing one contextlib @contextmanager instance across two with blocks -> the single-use generator raises RuntimeError on the second entry (and the analogous bug is a wrapper whose body-capture is consumed) -> instead call the factory fresh per use, or expose a ContextDecorator/class that creates a new instance per call.

Wrong move: letting the teardown error silently replace the body's error -> the root cause disappears from logs and monitoring -> instead follow an explicit policy — suppress the teardown error into the propagating one (Kotlin use, Java try-with-resources) or aggregate both (Spring rollback wrapping) — and never drop either.
